title: How To Handle Pesky, Advantageous Inattentiveness
author: Michael Linsin
summary: This piece addresses a narrow but common classroom management gap: well-managed classes that stay attentive while the teacher is actively speaking but drift the instant the teacher looks away, even briefly, to grab something or check a document camera. Linsin frames this as basic human nature -- when attention is unexpectedly interrupted, people seek stimulation elsewhere, comparable to a movie audience reacting when a projector breaks. His proposed fix is to make the expectation explicit rather than assumed: students must be directly taught that unless told otherwise, they are to wait patiently through any unplanned pause, and this expectation needs modeling and testing like any other routine. He recommends a deliberate practice technique in which the teacher fakes distraction (rummaging in a desk, fiddling with a cord) to test whether students hold the line, treating any side-talk as reason to enforce a normal consequence. The underlying argument is that even strong classroom managers leave time and momentum on the table by not addressing this specific, overlooked gap between the rules for active instruction and the rules for pauses.
points: Momentary teacher distraction (grabbing a document, checking a camera) reliably breaks student attention because unexpected interruption naturally sends people looking for stimulation elsewhere.
Explicitly teach students that they must wait patiently during unplanned pauses unless told they're free to talk -- don't assume this is obvious.
Model examples of unplanned pauses so students learn to recognize them, then test the expectation with staged distractions.
Deliberately fake losing your place or fumbling with something for a few days to see whether students hold their attention, and enforce a consequence if they don't.
quotes: Yet, the second you look away, even for a brief moment, you lose them and the momentum of your lesson. You’re able to bring them back, but it’s still frustrating.
It’s human nature. You see, whenever our attention is broken unexpectedly, we seek stimulation elsewhere. Think of being in a movie theater when the projector breaks.
This is why students start turning and looking around so quickly. They make eye contact with friends. They motion to each other. They side-talk or stare out the window.
The solution is to bring the issue out into the open. Unplanned pauses during lessons are going to happen. When they do, your students need to know exactly what is and isn’t okay.
To ensure the lesson is clear, you may want to be sneaky for a few days. Bluff, pretend, act as if you’re lost in thought or your attention is elsewhere and see if anyone side-talks.
This will strengthen their new habit, build academic discipline, and increase their ability to focus for longer and longer periods of time.
